intro: Mozart’s G minor minuet stamps across its three-beat bars, with the winds reinforcing the strings. In the Trio, G turns major and the orchestra breaks into smaller, gentler conversations.

sections.label: A · The G minor minuet
sections.mNote: Strong accents and overlapping string phrases

sections.label: B · Strings and winds in G major
sections.mNote: The Trio trades short phrases between the two groups

sections.label: A′ · The G minor minuet returns
sections.mNote: The full orchestra restores the opening accents

cues.title: A heavy-footed dance
cues.text: The strings begin with a rising, strongly accented phrase, reinforced by winds and horns. The minuet’s three beats are there, but the melody pulls across them. This is a splendidly awkward dance.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, bars 1–14. Marianne Williams Tobias describes the heavily accented opening: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Strings answer strings
cues.text: In the minuet’s second half, the parts pursue one another with fragments of the tune. The lower strings have their own say, pressing against the violins above them. The dance becomes an argument among several voices.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, bars 15–42: imitative writing in the minuet’s second strain.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: G major opens the room
cues.text: The Trio changes G minor to G major. Strings offer a gentler phrase and winds answer it; the horns warm the exchanges. After the minuet’s overlapping arguments, these groups give one another room to finish.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, Trio, bars 43–82. The change to G major is also documented in Tobias’s Indianapolis Symphony note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Why the Trio is called a Trio
cues.text: The middle dance is called the Trio because the seventeenth-century practice was to score it for three instruments. The name outlived the practice, and Mozart gives his Trio to strings and winds in changing groups.
cues.evidence: Harrap’s Illustrated Dictionary of Music and Musicians (1990): the section is known as the trio because it was originally scored for three instruments, a name that survived; Stephen Collins, Classical Music (1997), gives the same account (full-text excerpts seen, pages not recorded). The Trio’s scoring for changing groups: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III.

cues.title: An entry in July
cues.text: On 25 July 1788 Mozart enters this G minor symphony in his catalogue. The E♭ symphony is already entered, on 26 June; the C major Jupiter follows on 10 August. Three very different symphonies come out of one Viennese summer.
cues.evidence: Mozart’s thematic catalogue (British Library, Zweig MS 63), as listed in the chronological table in Otto Jahn, Life of Mozart, trans. P. D. Townsend (1882), vol. 3: K. 543 on 26 June, K. 550 on 25 July, K. 551 on 10 August 1788. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/43413 ; https://searcharchives.bl.uk/catalog/040-001945812

cues.title: Back to the minuet
cues.text: “Menuetto da capo”: Mozart sends the orchestra back to the first dance. G minor and the heavy accents return at once. The Trio’s sunny exchanges are over.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III: the Trio ends with the instruction Menuetto da capo, returning to bars 1–42.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A grand symphony in 1791
cues.text: In April 1791 the Vienna Tonkünstler-Societät gives its concerts, with Antonio Salieri conducting, and the programme announces “A Grand Symphony composed by Herr Mozart”. This G minor symphony later gains a second version with clarinets, and both versions survive.
cues.evidence: Otto Erich Deutsch, Mozart: A Documentary Biography (1965), prints the announcement “A Grand Symphony composed by Herr Mozart”; Ivor Keys, Mozart: His Music in His Life (1980), says Salieri conducted that part of the concert (full-text excerpts seen, pages not recorded; the announcement does not name the symphony). The two versions of K. 550, the second with clarinets, are printed in the Breitkopf & Härtel score (1880) and listed at https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.40_in_G_minor,_K.550_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus).

transitions.title: B♭ becomes B♮
transitions.to: B · Strings and winds in G major
transitions.how: The minuet closes in G minor; the Trio begins in G major. G remains the tonic, while B♭ becomes B♮. The full orchestra withdraws to let the strings begin a lighter phrase, with the wind answer following. There is no connecting passage.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, bars 42–50.

transitions.title: The orchestra stamps back in
transitions.from: B · Strings and winds in G major
transitions.to: A′ · The G minor minuet returns
transitions.how: The Trio closes in G major and the da capo instruction brings back the minuet in G minor. Winds and horns reinforce the strings again. The change from B♮ to B♭ restores the opening key, and the rising phrase resumes its forceful accents.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, end of Trio and Menuetto da capo.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/40 (1880), plate W.A.M. 550; parts common to both versions
source.locator: III. Menuetto and Trio, PDF pp. 30–33: minuet, bars 1–42; trio, bars 43–82; then the minuet returns. The edition prints both orchestral versions.

timeline.note: Winds and horns reinforce the strings’ sharply accented minuet.
Strings begin the trio’s gentler G major phrase.
Flute, oboes and bassoons answer the strings in the trio.
Horns join the trio’s exchanges between winds and strings.
The G minor minuet returns, with winds and horns reinforcing the accented strings.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
